chapter_theme: The second half of the marutham-kali: almost all dialogues between a wife and her straying husband, in which each of his excuses (a dream of Koodal's grove, a stay with the gods, a quail fight, a horse ride, a newly caught elephant, a bath in the Vaigai flood) is taken up and turned into the figure of the other woman; three poems (84 to 86) bring in the little son, whom the courtesans adorn and whom the mother nurses and teaches against his father; one (94) is a comic courtship of a dwarf and a hunchbacked woman; and the last two have the friend measure the husband, addressed as king, by the parasol, sceptre and drum and by the praises of truth, giving and justice.

84.reading: The wife, her unsucked milk swelling and spoiling like wind-felled mangoes, asks the attendant she sent to take her son round the temples in which of his father's women's houses he stopped; told that the women, seeing the boy under his parasol as the son of the man who forgets them, came out, held him in the street and decked him with gifts, she rails at the boy for wearing a stranger's ring engraved with the shark of Kama's banner, a sign meant for her, and his father's own bracelet, and ends by saying that neither the boy nor that woman is at fault, nor the father who is like a summer flood, only she who asked.
84.nuance: The other women are called the boy's mothers (தாயர், line 14), and their gift is a seal: the shark ring is Kama's banner, which the courtesan means to stamp on the father's chest so that the wife will read it (குறி அறிந்தேன்). The closing self-blame (யானே தவறு உடையேன்) is the bitterest line, since it clears everyone the wife has just accused.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband's other women reach the wife through her son

85.reading: The mother, listing her little son's ornaments (anklet bells, a coral string over his cloth, toy sword and axe and a bull pendant on his chest, a garland of pearls and gems), calls him off the toy chariot to drink at her breast, then shares the milk out in mockery: some for his father, who uses the lying bard as a fishhook to bind the hearts of women he wants, some for his other 'mothers', whose eyes weep after trusting his false oaths, and asks who invited the man who has come in on her fondling.
85.nuance: The poem is a lullaby turned into an indictment: the milk is divided into shares (நுந்தை பால், ஞாயர் பால், பாராட்டைப் பால்) as if the child owed each person in the father's life a mouthful. The last lines (32 to 36) are hard to construe and the shares there are not certain.

86.reading: The mother calls her little son, decked like a young tusker with a gold forehead plate and toy sword and axe, her 'war elephant', and tells him that he is like his father in beauty, may he be like him in winning battles, in a sceptre straight as daylight and in giving to those who seek lasting wealth, but not like him in leaving the women who trusted him to waste; then, as the father appears from hiding and asks for the boy, she refuses, but the boy slips her hand and leaps onto his father's chest like a lion climbing a cliff, 'son of a loveless man'.
86.nuance: The triple refrain (ஒத்தி... ஒவ்வாதி) splits the father into his public virtues (valour, justice, giving) and his private fault, and asks the son to inherit only the first; the son's leap to the father's chest answers her at once. 'Son of a man who is no man' (மகன் அல்லான் பெற்ற மகன், also in 84) is the household's verdict on the father.

thinai_evidence.note: a husband who leaves the women who trusted him

comparisons.tenor: the boy's three-strand ornament on his head, like a young tusker's forehead plate

87.reading: The wife tells her husband to keep off and not touch her hair; he asks how she can be angry with one who is her own body parted from her, when he has done no wrong; she answers that he has his freedom and is gone in the blink of an eye, and the fault is hers for sulking at a man who knows his place; then she tells her heart that sulking at a shameless man who left her weeping is useless, and that it will see her give up all complaint so her sleepless, tearful eyes may rest.
87.nuance: 'You have got release' (நீ வீடு பெற்றாய்) borrows the word for liberation to mock the husband's freedom from the household. The last speech, to the heart, gives up the quarrel not because he is forgiven but because sulking needs a partner with shame. Lines 11, 12, 15 and 16 are missing from the sangamtamil.com text.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's sulk at a husband who is free to stray

comparisons.tenor: the wife, to him like his own body parted from him

88.reading: The wife tells her husband, his shoulders thick with pollen from the hair of fine women, to keep off, asking what he is to her; he says he cannot live without her eyes; she points to the evidence on him, nail scratches and tooth marks like the holes a spotted crab makes in the wet bank, a faded garland, a chest reddened by angry women; and when he offers to swear his innocence she refuses, asking on whom his false oath, if it turns into a striking spirit, will fall.
88.nuance: Her refusal of the oath is also care: an oath sworn falsely becomes an அணங்கு that strikes, and she asks who it would strike (யார் மேல் விளியுமோ), meaning him. The crab's holes in the mud bank are a marutham image used as forensic evidence.

89.reading: The wife asks who this is that grabs her hair, a trick fit for a townsman's lordship, and tells him to go back; he says her sulking is like one head of a two-headed bird fighting the other and asks how his life can last; she tells him not to wear her out with his tales like a ghoul telling stories to the forest goddess; he says that when a king is angry there is no remedy, and he has done no wrong; she tells her heart to watch this shameless man turn tail, for if pressed he will fall at their feet confessing.
89.nuance: The two-headed bird with one life is the husband's best argument: a quarrel between them is self-harm. She answers it with an image of deceit (the ghoul's tales to the goddess of the wild), and her final aside expects not reconciliation but his collapse at her feet.

90.reading: The wife tells her husband she has found out his trickery and not to touch her; when he asks what fault she saw, she tells it as a string of questions: in last night's midnight rain a woman with shining shoulders came, her anklet ringing, and kicked his door, he rose at once and went, she tore his garland, he bowed to her small feet saying he was not wicked; is that enough? He asks whether she dreamed it; she says his oaths are not what they were and he has many homes; he begs to enjoy her beauty, and she yields, asking whether women whose hearts cannot hold out can say they will not bear his wrongs.
90.nuance: The refrain அமையுமோ ('is that enough?') turns a reported scene into a cross-examination, each question adding one act. His defence that she dreamed it is answered by repeating his own words back (கண்ட கனவு). The close is a surrender framed as a reproach: the wife's lack of நிறை, not his innocence, ends the quarrel.

91.reading: The wife tells her husband that the garland of lilies, jasmine and anicham he loves was crushed by his women's anger and asks him to adorn her with it; he asks why she is angry from mere suspicion and offers to prove his innocence by an oath before a god; she says she knows his oath and lists the bangle scars, the nail scratches, the crumpled garland and smeared sandal that the street's women left on him, says she has given up the fight and tells him to go; when he offers to bow, she says that since her heart melts at the sight of him whatever he does, he need not trouble to please her.
91.nuance: The last argument turns her weakness into his licence: because her heart gives way whenever she sees him, he has no reason to behave (பேணாய் நீ பெட்பச் செயல்). The mullai jasmine in a marutham garland is only an ornament.

thinai_evidence.note: the husband returns marked by other women

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi

92.reading: The husband tells his wife of a dream in which he went to the grove on the Vaigai's bank at Koodal and saw women gathered like a flock of swans resting on the Himalaya at dusk; when one pulled down a flowering creeper the bees broke out like a fort the Pandya stormed and swarmed them as if to feast on their beauty, and he describes each woman's plight, until they fled tangled like wind-blown creepers; the wife says he is dressing up in a dream his women's sulks and his bowing to them; he answers that the dream will come true when the koels call to lovers 'united, do not part; parted, unite', and the men and women of Koodal sport in the groves to welcome spring for Kama.
92.nuance: The opening maxim (lines 3 to 9) says that some things no one can give himself, among them lovers' parting and union; the dream then stages a crowd of women each undone by bees, which the wife reads as a coded account of his own affairs. His last move recasts the dream as a prophecy of the spring festival, where all couples unite, so his straying becomes the season's law. Lines 6 to 9 are compressed and their construction is not sure.

93.reading: The wife asks her husband, his sandal smeared and marked, what he saw to come home at night; he says he stayed with the gods who help a household; she asks which god, since many deer-like women act as gods to him, and runs through them: the god who named their wedding hour? a lie told with tongue pressed and head bent; did he see the goddess who came to his house to be plucked, the one with binding eyes to whom he offered flowers, the one who sang of the red-speared slayer of Sur with him on the hill through the rains? which of them marked his chest? she believes him; let him go, or all the long-haired gods on his chest may be put out.
93.nuance: The whole poem plays on கடவுள், god and goddess-like woman: his excuse of worship is taken literally and turned into an inventory of women, each 'god' defined by a rite (pluck, flower offering, songs to Murugan on the hill). Line 2 calls the husband himself பரத்தை, the masculine use.

94.reading: A dwarf courts a hunchbacked woman in the palace: he calls her lovely and says her bent body has made him sick with love; she mocks him as an owl's brat, a dice board stood on end, a heap smaller than black gram, asks whether he has no women of his own and whether a hunchback's birth is lower than his; he asks at least to embrace her from the side, since from the front her chest and from behind her hump prevent him; when she follows him all the same he mocks her walk, and at last they agree, he swearing by the king's feet and she asking him to come under the grove so the palace will not laugh at two goblins dancing.
94.nuance: A comic poem: the insults are similes in the high style turned on bodies the tradition does not allow to be lovers, which is why the thinai is perunthinai though the colophon files it under marutham. The two still use the lovers' forms: the oath by the king's foot, the fear of being laughed at, the tryst in the grove. Lines 13 to 43 are missing from the sangamtamil.com text, and several words (குறு வட்டா, தகடு உருவ) are rare.

95.reading: The wife stops her husband at the door, saying he has lost his way to the fragrant-haired women's houses; he says he only watched a quail fight; she agrees he saw quail fights: a 'gift fight' to the bard's lute that left unhealed wounds, a 'decoy fight' in which a woman held his garland in her beak and would not let go, leaving wet wounds on his shoulders, a 'clinging fight' that his face betrays; he offers to swear on her body; she says he cannot tell truth from lies; he admits he is caught and asks for grace; she says she will grant it, and tells him to go and play with his bard and tend all the quails he trained, which pine since he left them.
95.nuance: The husband's alibi gives her the metaphor: each kind of quail fight she names is a kind of love bout, and the wounds are its evidence. Her pardon ends on the quails themselves: he is sent back to the birds he trained, which suffer when he leaves them, so the wife speaks for her rivals too.

96.reading: The wife asks her husband, with torn cloth, smeared sandal and slipping garland, where he has been; he says he went riding a horse; she says she knows that horse, describes a woman as a horse with mane, plume and harness of jewels, which he rode on the moonlit terrace of a white mansion, asks whether it was the horse that scratched him like the swept courtyard of Madurai and bit him, and concludes that it is not the caparisoned horse he married by dharma but a wind-horse brought by the bard's go-between, and tells him to ride it and be the courtesan's groom for ever.
96.nuance: The metaphor sets two horses against each other: the caparisoned one married with rites (the wife) and the wind-horse that arrives on the bard's errand (the courtesan); the last line makes the husband no rider but a groom, the courtesan's servant.

97.reading: The wife, mocked for scolding though she never spoke harshly, asks where her husband went after coming to her door at dawn; he says a new elephant had fallen into their net and he stayed to see it; she agrees, describing the elephant: it bathed in powder and drank toddy, wore a tilaka for a forehead plate and painted breasts for tusks, smiled with pearl teeth, leaned at the door post, tripped and caught men with its soft arms and swallowed the beauty of those who saw it; why pretend he saw it only today, when he rode it on festival days and after drinking, while his women stood by like little mahouts; let him beware when it is in must.
97.nuance: Each part of a war elephant's gear is matched to the courtesan's adornment (forehead plate to tilaka, tusks to painted breasts, goad and bells to ornaments), and the wild elephant who should be caught is the one catching men. His wives as 'little mahouts' who do not complain (சிறு பாகர்) puts the wife among them.

98.reading: The wife asks who her husband is to enter her house, a bee seeking new flowers whose philandering is the song of every chariot street, now caught; he swears he stayed to bathe in the new flood of the Vaigai; she agrees he bathed in a flood, a woman whose hair was its sand-ripples, whose eyes its leaping carp, whose flowers its surface, who broke the dam of modesty at noon, with the bard as his raft; that he bathed in secret fearing the gossip she would hear, and the flood, with frowning waves and ringing anklets, swept him off so that he has not yet reached the shore; when he swears by a god that he bathed in the Pandya's Vaigai, she warns him not to let his chariot sink in the soft sand, where no one will pull him out, and make the women laugh.
98.nuance: Each feature of the river is mapped to a woman (ripples to hair, carp to eyes, the floating flowers to her garlands, the broken embankment to her lost modesty), so his alibi becomes the confession. The closing warning about sinking in sand keeps the river metaphor to the end.

99.reading: The friend tells the hero, addressed as a king whose rightness keeps the rains coming as a mother watches her infant: you hold your parasol as the shade of virtue; did she fall outside its shade, she whose brow is pale with longing? your sceptre proclaims truth; did she fall outside its working, she who is weary of living from love's sickness? your drum proclaims protection; is she beyond it, whose bamboo-smooth shoulders are losing their beauty? Like an eye that sees far things but not its own scar, has it kept you from seeing that leaving my friend was cruel?
99.nuance: The three royal insignia, parasol, sceptre and drum, each promise to cover all subjects, and the refrain asks whether the wife alone fell outside them. The closing simile, the eye that sees far but not the scar beside it, makes his blindness to her a defect of the same faculty that makes him a good ruler.

100.reading: The friend tells the hero, a king of famous drum, harsh to foes like the sun that rises from the sea to drive off darkness and cool like the moon to those under his parasol, that his praise as one who like the great ascetic never lies will be ruined when she who trusted his word weeps, his praise as one who like the rain never disappoints a suppliant will be ruined when her bangles slip, and his praise as one who does justice like Death weighing lives will be ruined when her face pales; she who lost her beauty is the one he took as partner; need I reproach him, who removes the sorrow of people like me?
100.nuance: The three praises (truth, giving, justice) are each said to be undone by one sign of the wife's wasting: tears, slipping bangles, pallor. The last line is irony: the man who relieves everyone's suffering is asked whether he needs to be told of hers.

links.note: In Akananuru 16 the wife meets a courtesan cuddling her son in the chariot street and asks 'are you his mother too?'; in Kalittokai 84 the husband's women, the boy's 'mothers' (தாயர்), stop him in the street and load him with gifts, and the wife reads the shark ring as a message.
links.teaches: The two poems show that the son in the street was a fixed channel between wife and courtesan: the Akananuru wife disarms the rival by granting her a mother's place, while the Kalittokai wife finds that the same motherly gesture is used to send her a sign, so the courtesy of Akananuru 16 had a hostile counterpart.

links.note: Purananuru 312 assigns bearing the son to the mother and making him worthy (சான்றோன் ஆக்குதல்) to the father; in Kalittokai 86 the mother herself teaches the son which of his father's qualities to copy and which to refuse.
links.teaches: Read together, they show the puram division of duties failing inside the house: when the father is the bad example, the mother takes over his task of forming the son, sorting his public virtues from his private fault, which the puram poem's neat allocation never anticipates.

links.note: Kural 70 says a son repays his father by making people ask what penance the father did; Kalittokai 86 has the mother wish the son to resemble the father in valour, justice and giving but not in leaving women.
links.teaches: The Kural assumes the father is the standard the son's goodness reflects back on, while the akam mother makes the son's goodness a correction of the father, so the same likeness that honours a father in the Kural reproaches him in the Kalittokai.

links.note: In Kural 1259 the woman went to sulk and embraced him when she saw her heart joining him; in Kalittokai 87 the wife tells her heart that sulking at a shameless man is pointless and gives up her complaint.
links.teaches: Both wives abandon the sulk through the heart, but for opposite reasons: in the Kural the heart's desire overrides her, in the Kalittokai the heart concludes that a man without shame cannot be moved by sulking, so ending an oodal can be resignation as well as longing.

links.note: In Kural 1313 the man complains that even if he wears a garland she accuses him of wearing it for another woman; in Kalittokai 88 the wife points to his faded garland, the pollen of other women's hair and the nail marks on him.
links.teaches: The Kural presents the wife's suspicion of a garland as groundless jealousy from the man's side, while the Kalittokai wife reads the same evidence correctly, so the couplet's comic complaint rests on an akam scene in which the garland really was a sign.

links.note: Kural 1325 has a faultless man delight in being kept from his beloved's arms; in Kalittokai 89 the husband says he has done no wrong (தீதோ இலேன்) and the wife calls the claim deceit and expects him to fall at her feet confessing.
links.teaches: The Kural builds the pleasure of oodal on the man's real innocence, while the Kalittokai shows the same plea of innocence as the stock defence of a straying husband, so the couplet's playful exclusion presupposes a faultlessness that akam wives treat as the thing in dispute.

links.note: Kural 1260 asks whether those whose hearts melt like fat in fire can say 'we will join and then sulk'; Kalittokai 90 ends with the wife asking whether women whose hearts cannot hold restraint (நிறை ஆற்றா நெஞ்சு) can say they will not bear his wrongs.
links.teaches: The Kalittokai gives the couplet's rhetorical question a full case: a detailed charge of a night visit, his dream defence and his plea, so that the wife's collapse comes after she has proved him guilty, showing that the melting heart of the Kural overrides evidence and not only pride.

links.note: In Kural 1288 the woman says his chest is to her as liquor is to drinkers, though it does shameful harm; Kalittokai 91 ends with the wife saying her heart melts when she sees him whatever wrong he does, so he need not try to please her.
links.teaches: The Kural states the compulsion as the woman's confession, while the Kalittokai draws its consequence for the man: because she always yields, he has no motive to behave, so the wife's helplessness becomes part of the reason the straying continues.

links.note: Paripadal 5 opens by hailing the spear that cut down Sur; in Kalittokai 93 one of the husband's 'goddesses' sang of the red-speared slayer of Sur with him on the hill through the rains.
links.teaches: The pair shows the Murugan hymn in two settings: in the Paripadal it is temple praise, while the Kalittokai places the same theme in a lovers' pastime on the hill in the rainy season, so devotional song at Murugan's hill was also an occasion for courtship that the wife can use as evidence.

links.note: In Akananuru 296 the friend refuses the man who bathed in the great Vaigai with a dark girl and comes home with his chest still wet; in Kalittokai 98 the man claims he only bathed in the Vaigai's new flood and the wife turns the flood itself into the courtesan.
links.teaches: The Akananuru records water play in the Vaigai as the plain occasion of an affair and its gossip, while the Kalittokai husband offers that same occasion as an innocent excuse and the wife answers by making the river a figure for the woman, so a known scene of straying becomes the material for the wife's metaphor.

links.note: Purananuru 35 tells Killivalavan that his tall umbrella is not for shade from the sun but to shelter suffering subjects, and that rain comes in the land of the just sceptre; Kalittokai 99 asks the husband, addressed as king, whether his wife fell outside the shade of the parasol he calls virtue's shade and the working of his sceptre.
links.teaches: The friend in the Kalittokai uses the same counsel a puram poet gave a king, that the parasol exists to shade those who suffer, and turns it on the household, showing that the akam poets could hold a husband to the standard of kingship and find him failing his nearest subject.

links.note: Kural 559 says that if the ruler bends justice the sky withholds rain; Kalittokai 99 praises the king for rains that come by his rightness and then asks whether his wife alone lies outside that rightness.
links.teaches: The Kural ties rain to the king's public justice only, while the Kalittokai grants the rain and still finds injustice at home, so the friend shows that the doctrine's measure of a ruler can be met in full while a wife is wronged.

links.note: Purananuru 55 wishes the Pandya the heat of the sun, the coolness of the moon and the giving of the rain; Kalittokai 100 praises the husband, as king, with the sun's harshness to foes, the moon's coolness to those under his parasol and the rain's giving, then says each praise is ruined by his wife's tears, bangles and pallor.
links.teaches: The akam friend takes the stock triad of royal praise found in the Purananuru and makes each term hostage to a woman's body, showing that the same encomium could be turned into a reproach by asking whether its subject meets it at home.
